titre: Only 14% of American silent films survive in their original format
accroche: In 2013, the Library of Congress counts the eleven thousand American silent films released between 1912 and 1929, and tallies those that still exist.
contenu_vulgarise:
In a barn, long after Mary Pickford's death, someone finds a perforated, scratched, nearly unreadable reel. It is Their First Misunderstanding, a 1911 film, the very first in which her name appears in the credits. She is eighteen and will soon be one of the highest-paid actresses in the country. The film survived by accident; most of those shot the same decade were not so lucky.

## Eleven thousand titles, a third survive

In September 2013, the Library of Congress publishes the first complete survey of what remains of American silent cinema. The historian David Pierce cross-references the American Film Institute catalog, which lists 10,919 silent feature films released in the United States between 1912 and 1929, with the collections of film archives and private archives around the world. The result: 14% of these films, about 1,575 titles, survive complete in their 35 mm release format. A further 11% survive only in degraded form, as a foreign print or a reduced format such as 16 mm, and 5% are incomplete. In other words, a little under a third of the output has made it through the century in one form or another; more than two-thirds have vanished. The nitrate film stock of the era, highly flammable and chemically unstable, explains part of that; the indifference of the studios, which had no commercial use for a silent film once sound had taken hold, accounts for the rest.

## What this changes

The report shows not only how much is missing, it also shows what allowed some films to remain. Mary Pickford personally financed the preservation of her own negatives: of her 48 feature films, only eight, all from the very beginning of her career, are lost. Tom Mix, the first big star of the Western, did not have that control over his films: 85% have disappeared. The survival of a silent film was therefore anything but chance: it depended on who held the rights, and on that person's willingness to pay for preservation, decades before any law obliged anyone to. Part of what survives, moreover, was found only abroad: the Czech Republic alone holds the largest collection of American silent films outside the United States, proof that these prints had traveled long before anyone thought of protecting them at home.

repere.texte: Of the 10,919 American silent feature films released between 1912 and 1929, 14% (about 1,575 titles) survive today complete in their original 35 mm format. A further 11% survive only in degraded form, a foreign version or a copy in a lower-quality format, and 5% are incomplete: in all, a little under a third has made it through the century in one form or another.
repere.source: David Pierce, The Survival of American Silent Feature Films: 1912-1929, CLIR / Library of Congress, 2013

carte.punch: More than two out of three American silent films have vanished.
carte.idee: In 2013, a Library of Congress survey establishes that of 10,919 American silent films released between 1912 and 1929, only 14% survive complete in their original format. Less than a third survived, often because a rights holder paid for their preservation.

quiz.question: According to the survey published by the Library of Congress in 2013, why did some American silent films survive better than others?
choix: Because the studios systematically kept a copy of every film in a fireproof vault
Because the nitrate film stock of films shot before 1920 withstood time better than that of later films
Because some rights holders, like Mary Pickford, personally financed the preservation of their own films
Because a 1929 federal law required the mandatory deposit of a copy with the Library of Congress
quiz.explication: The report notes no systematic fireproof vault, no mandatory deposit law in 1929, and no difference in chemical stability by decade of shooting: it shows instead that survival depended on who held the rights. Mary Pickford financed the preservation of her negatives herself and lost only eight of her 48 films; Tom Mix, without that control, lost 85% of his.

The instability of nitrate film stock and the studios' indifference once sound had taken hold

The systematic theft of reels by private collectors
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Nitrate film stock, highly flammable and chemically unstable, explains part of the losses; the indifference of the studios, which had no commercial use for a silent film once sound had taken hold, accounts for the rest.
